title: When the stars retreat
hook: glorify Him when you rise and at the retreat of the stars (52:48–49)

segments.voice: Yesterday, At-Tur, and your line was by the mount. Which book did you open slowly, and what was the line? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

At the very end of the night, the sky is still dark, but something has already shifted. The faint stars go first. Then the brighter ones, one by one, as if someone were walking through a house turning off lamps. Birds start before there's any light to speak of, and the whole change is over quickly. Surah At-Tur ends exactly there, at that hour, and it tells the Prophet ﷺ what to do with it.
screen: `THE STARS GO OUT, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The last two verses of At-Tur begin with comfort. Wait patiently for your Lord's decree, it says to the Prophet, for you are in Our sight. The Arabic is bi-a'yunina, literally within Our eyes: watched over, never out of view. Then the instruction, in Pickthall's translation: "And in the night-time also hymn His praise, and at the setting of the stars." Idbar an-nujum: the turning back of the stars, their retreat as dawn comes. Three times for glorifying, tasbih, are named across these two verses: when you rise, in the night, and as the stars withdraw. Commentators connected idbar an-nujum with the two short units of prayer before the dawn prayer, the sunnah of Fajr. A report attributed to Ibn 'Abbas says so, and other commentators followed him. And the hadith tradition treats those two units with unusual tenderness. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says the two units before dawn are better than the world and everything in it. 'A'ishah reported, in Bukhari, that he was never more regular in any voluntary prayer than in those two. Notice the shape of the verse. It doesn't say glorify Him in the bright, busy middle of the day. It says, in effect: at the edges. When you've just risen and when the night is letting go. The hours when nobody needs you yet. Subhanallah is the phrase of tasbih: glory be to Allah, far above every flaw. Said as the stars fade, it's a way of meeting the day before the day starts asking things of you.
screen: `BI-A'YUNINA: WITHIN OUR EYES.` · `IDBAR AN-NUJUM: THE STARS TURN BACK.` · `THE TWO UNITS BEFORE DAWN.` · `PRAISE AT THE EDGES OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The practice is a tasbih before dawn. You can rehearse it now, and keep it tomorrow. Sit, and breathe. Picture waking before the light, the sky just beginning to thin. With each slow breath, say subhanallah quietly, glory to Allah. Count on your fingers if you like. If you don't pray, simply hold the picture of the stars going out, one by one, and let your breath slow with them. Set an alarm for a few minutes before sunrise tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Tasbih: glorifying God, named three times at the edges of night and day in Surah At-Tur's last verses, as the stars withdraw. Today's word.
Your line: as the stars fade. Tomorrow, try to be awake as the last stars go, and give the first minute to praise or to stillness. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Many Muslims pray two short voluntary units before the obligatory dawn prayer, and say subhanallah, often thirty-three times, after prayers and in the early morning.

what it means: praise at the moment night lets go, read as the two units of prayer before dawn.
what a scholar hears: idbar is the turning back; Ibn 'Abbas's reading; Muslim 725 and 'A'ishah's report in Bukhari show how much these two units mattered.
